item.title: Overlooked No More: Patricia Douglas, Who Challenged Hollywood’s Culture of Abuse
item.description:
This article is part of Overlooked, a series of obituaries about remarkable people whose deaths, beginning in 1851, went unreported in The Times.

In May 1937, a 20-year-old extra and dancer named Patricia Douglas was invited to appear in a movie produced by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the biggest movie studio in Hollywood.

When she showed up on location at the ranch of the producer Hal Roach in Culver City, Calif., she discovered that there was no film shoot. Instead, she later said, she and more than 100 other young women — many of whom were minors — had been summoned to entertain men attending MGM’s annual sales convention.

Douglas later testified in court that during the event, one MGM salesman harassed her, then two men held her down and forced her to drink liquor. Later, she said, the salesman assaulted and raped her in the parking lot.

She reported the attack to prosecutors, pursued a criminal case and sued the studio executives she believed were responsible. She later said MGM mounted a campaign to discredit her, and witnesses mysteriously recanted their earlier statements. A grand jury declined to indict the salesman, her civil suit was dismissed and her story fell out of public memory.

Douglas later said MGM had mounted a campaign to discredit her and had succeeded, and she was blackballed by Hollywood. Years before the #MeToo movement of the late 2010s transformed the way sexual abuse in Hollywood was discussed, Douglas’s story re-emerged because of a curious reporter who had happened upon the case in the course of other research.

“I see her as the Rosa Parks of rape culture,” David Stenn, the reporter, said in an interview. “She stood up against the culture of silence when no one else did.”

Stenn unearthed Douglas’s story in 2003 for a Vanity Fair article, “It Happened One Night at MGM,” and a 2007 film documentary, “Girl 27,” a title taken from the number assigned to Douglas in MGM’s call sheet for the supposed movie shoot — a document he discovered in the Hal Roach archives at the University of Southern California.

Stenn researched the Douglas case for years, digging up grand jury affidavits with sworn testimonies, along with black-and-white film footage of the salesmen arriving at the ranch, where they were welcomed by MGM’s studio chief, Louis B. Mayer. The event was billed as a Wild West show, and the women were given cowgirl costumes to wear.

Karen McNally, the editor of the 2026 book “Women in Hollywood’s Dream Factory: Tales of Inequality, Abuse, and Resistance,” said in an interview that the circumstances surrounding Douglas’s assault were hardly unusual in the 1930s studio system. Young women were routinely brought in to entertain men at industry events, leaving them vulnerable to abuse, she said.

“If you’re repeating the behavior in this manner, which is quite blatant and intentional — that’s a system,” she said.

Patricia Douglas was born Dorothy Shellenberger on March 24, 1917, in Kansas City, Mo., to William Shellenberger, a chauffeur, and Mildred Kritser, who Douglas later estimated had been “married eight times.”

The family moved to Los Angeles in 1920; her parents divorced in 1928. Kritser was a gown designer who “kind of disappeared,” Douglas said, moving into an apartment in Beverly Hills while Dorothy went to live with her grandparents.

At the time, young women from across the country were flocking to Los Angeles, lured by the promise of Hollywood and the opportunities it seemed to offer, especially amid the Great Depression.

“It’s kind of like, ‘Go west, young woman!’ because women have opportunities in Hollywood that they don’t have in other places,” said McNally, who is a professor of American film, television and cultural history at London Metropolitan University. “It’s advertised as something new and wonderful. These young women would have been running around auditioning everywhere.”

At around 14, Dorothy dropped out of school to work as a dancer and changed her name to Patricia Douglas. At 16, she appeared, uncredited, in the 1933 Bert Wheeler-Robert Woolsey comedy “So This Is Africa” and the musical “Gold Diggers of 1933.”

Douglas was in her mid-80s when Stenn tracked her down in Las Vegas, where she was living at the time. With her permission, he recorded their phone conversations for months. He eventually persuaded her to sit for an on-camera interview in 2002.

She told Stenn that the party hosted by MGM was on May 5, 1937, the final night of a four-day convention. A Chicago-based salesman named David Ross approached Douglas on the dance floor. “He kept pestering me to teach him how to truck,” she said. “That was the dance at the time.” He tried every way he could “to get his hands around me,” and eventually she left the dance floor and returned to her table.

There were cases of scotch and champagne, but when Douglas said she didn’t drink alcohol, two salesmen forced her to, by holding her nose and pouring the liquor into her mouth.

She ran to the washroom to vomit, then went out to the parking lot for air. That was when Ross knocked her down, dragged her to his car and raped her, she said.

“The only thing I can remember is this David Ross’s face. It was in my nightmares for many years,” she said in the film documentary. “I could not get him off my mind and what he had done to me. He took my innocence. You can never get that back.”

Her account of the incident became headline news almost immediately after it happened. The Daily Times, a Chicago tabloid paper, ran a full-page headline, “Wild Film Party,” and a sub-headline, “Assault Told by Girl, 17,” for a story that included her name and photo, incorrectly reporting her age as three years younger than she was.

Subsequent news about developments in the case appeared in papers across the country, including The Los Angeles Times, with stories resorting to euphemisms like “ravished” or “outraged” instead of “rape.”

“Rape was literally a four-letter word in the 1930s,” Stenn said. “They wouldn’t print it in the newspapers."

Ross called Douglas’s claims “absurd, ridiculous” and Mayer’s personal attorney defended the salesman in the case, Stenn said.

When the grand jury declined to indict Ross, Douglas refused to let the matter end there. She sued Ross and other studio executives in Los Angeles Superior Court, accusing them of conspiring to “defile, debauch, and seduce” her for “the immoral and sensual gratification of male guests,” according to legal documents. She sought $500,000 in damages — more than $11 million in today’s dollars.

The suit was dismissed in February 1938. The next day, she filed an identical suit in federal court, arguing that the assault had violated her civil rights. It was, Stenn wrote in Vanity Fair, apparently the first time a woman had made rape the basis of a federal civil-rights case. That case, too, was ultimately dismissed because both lawyers failed to show up in court.

In “Girl 27,” Stenn described a cover-up campaign led by executives at MGM, which implicated the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s office and the doctor who had examined Douglas after the attack. Even an eyewitness who had helped her when she emerged from the bushes, crying and bleeding, later denied having seen anything.

“What she did had no real precedent, and she did it in a vacuum when there was no support on any level, no legal protections for women, and such a situation was considered unspeakable,” Stenn said in an interview.

A representative from Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns MGM’s film library from the 1930s, said the company did not have “anyone who can speak on the matter.” The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s office could not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Douglas married and divorced three times and had a daughter from her first marriage. Douglas died on Nov. 11, 2003, in Las Vegas. She was 86.

McNally said that very few cases of harassment and assault in the film industry came to light at the time, unless the woman involved was famous. Although there’s evidence that stars like Lana Turner, Judy Garland, and Shirley Temple faced sexual harassment or assault on the job, those stories often went public long after the incidents occurred.

The fact that Douglas’s case became so widely known was also unusual, McNally said. “Her case was in the press at the time,” she said. “It was headline news, and it was out there at the time, and then just forgotten.”

item.title: Universal’s New Coaster Is a Scream. That’s the Problem.
item.description:
After three years of painstaking work, Universal Studios Hollywood recently pulled off a seemingly impossible feat: It built a 72-mile-per-hour, looping roller coaster with spinning “Fast & Furious” cars — that barely makes a sound.

Universal had good reason to obsess. Residential neighborhoods press against the theme park, and its own movie studio operates alongside it. To silence the ride, Universal went so far as to fill the 4,100-foot track with pea gravel, muting the vibrations that give coasters their roar.

When riderless testing began last month, residents in nearby Toluca Lake were delighted, with several calling the attraction “whisper quiet.”

Then came the riders.

Every 30 seconds or so, for 10 hours straight, according to interviews with more than a dozen homeowners, the air is now filled with the sound of humans who fear they’re in mortal peril.

“Screams — bloodcurdling screams,” said Craig Strong, who has lived near Universal Studios Hollywood for 25 years. “Some people can hear it inside their homes with the windows closed.”

One angry resident said she could hear the screams even after removing her hearing aids. Another worried about her livelihood: She teaches meditation from home.

“We’re accustomed to some theme park noise, but the screaming is new, and it’s impossible to tune out,” said Judith Angel, who has lived nearby for 38 years. “Our brains are designed to respond to screaming. It’s biology.”

Neighbors have one demand. Universal must somehow find a way to muffle its very happy customers.

It would be easy to dismiss this as another chapter in the long history of neighborhood noise disputes in America. But the predicament underscores Universal’s longstanding challenge — how do you expand one of the world’s busiest theme parks when homes and a working movie studio sit almost on top of it? Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift was supposed to demonstrate that Universal had figured out how to overcome constraints.

Comcast, which owns the park, has been counting on Hollywood Drift to revive attendance and compete with an expanding Disneyland to the south. Universal Studios Hollywood attracted 8.8 million visitors in 2024, down 10 percent from 2023, according to the Themed Entertainment Association, which has yet to release 2025 figures.

Jason Armstrong, Comcast’s chief financial officer, told analysts in July that business had improved, “though we do not expect a more meaningful improvement until the new Fast & Furious roller coaster opens.” Universal declined to say how much the ride cost. Theme park analysts say attractions of this size and complexity typically cost $200 million or more.

As of Friday, Hollywood Drift was still in “technical rehearsals,” according to Universal, with no opening date beyond what the company has said since February: “summer.” Universal declined to make executives available for interviews but said in an email to neighborhood groups that audio measurements showed the ride was “operating in compliance with sound ordinance requirements.”

Universal added that it was nonetheless “exploring additional measures to further lessen sound levels experienced in adjacent neighborhoods.” Workers have begun expanding a sound wall. Universal also said it would stop running the coaster at 7 p.m. during the testing period and at 10 p.m. during Halloween Horror Nights, when the park is open as late as 2 a.m.

Universal took screaming into account from the start. Using computer modeling, ride designers mapped where screams were most likely to occur and incorporated defenses. Hollywood Drift was built with two “scream screens,” half-pipe-like glass shields meant to “encase sound at the source,” Universal has said. There is also a 940-foot sound wall made with Acoustiblok, a dense, rubbery material used to insulate buildings near airports.

The coaster’s spinning cars were enlisted: Universal said they were programmed to turn riders’ mouths away from nearby homes at “key scream moments.”

Universal even mounted speakers near the coaster site and played recordings of a roller coaster at a Florida park. Engineers wanted to study how sound traveled down the steep hillside.

What worked in computer models, however, has proved less effective against actual lungs.

Now residents are making noise of their own, flooding elected officials with complaints and demanding that neighborhood councils, which serve as conduits to City Hall, get involved. One coalition said it had hired its own sound consultants. Another said it had approached law firms to find out what representation would cost.

“I have a feeling this isn’t going to be over anytime soon,” said Leonard R. Garner, who has lived next to Universal for 28 years.

Toluca Lake was developed in the 1920s and became a Hollywood haven, attracting stars like Bette Davis and moguls like Roy O. Disney. The entertainment connection endures: Ray Romano and Rick Dees, the radio countdown king, have made their homes there. Toluca Lake also boasts the Lakeside Golf Club, an ultraexclusive private course.

As local news outlets have reported on the noise complaints in recent weeks, social media has predictably lit up with variations on “wealthy people whining.” But residents take issue with the caricature of their neighborhood as a gilded realm of the entitled and the well connected.

“This impacts people of all income levels — we have all types of housing,” said Kevin Dees, Rick’s son, who grew up in Toluca Lake and now sells real estate there. “Income level also has nothing to do with whether you deserve to have quiet in your own home.”

To the horror of residents, roller coaster enthusiasts have joined the pile-on, with some vowing to scream even louder.

“No one is against having fun, and no one wants the roller coaster taken away,” Mr. Strong said. “We just want it to be quieter.”

Expansion has long brought Universal into conflict with its neighbors. After residents pushed back against a development plan in the 1990s, the company cut its proposal nearly in half. Later that decade, Universal bought a string of homes along its perimeter and converted them into corporate housing.

Theme parks are generally easier neighbors when they don’t have neighbors. Disney World in Florida has 25,000 acres to itself. Dollywood occupies a wooded valley in eastern Tennessee.

In contrast, Universal Studios Hollywood is squeezed across multiple levels of a hillside in the middle of Los Angeles. It did not start as a theme park. Rather, it grew out of tours that Universal began offering at its movie studio in 1964. Over the decades, Universal mostly added rides that were either indoors or relatively modest in scale.

Hollywood Drift is a dramatic departure — Universal’s most aggressive coaster anywhere and, theme park experts say, the most anticipated new ride of the year.

The challenge is making it peacefully coexist with the neighborhoods around it. Residents have floated ideas ranging from roofs on the coaster cars to sound-muffling helmets. During the Covid-19 pandemic, one Japanese park, concerned about respiratory droplets, asked riders to “please scream inside your heart.”

Universal, as it sometimes does with soon-to-open attractions, has been inviting neighbors to come for a ride. Mr. Garner, 73, accepted. “There’s a point when it’s accelerating up a hill and then it drops, and you feel like you could come out of your seat,” he texted a reporter.

Did he scream?

“Hell, yeah!”

item.title: For Gen Z, Building Wealth Is in the Stock Market, Not the Housing Market
item.description:
Kana Cummings got into personal finance in 2020, when “the world was kind of crumbling,” she said.

It was her junior year of college, and some students had organized a personal finance workshop to help quell anxieties during the coronavirus panic.

“It was such an inescapable time,” said Ms. Cummings, 26, who lives in Cleveland. “I think people were like, ‘We really need to be thinking about these things kind of early.’”

After taking the workshop, she opened a Roth individual retirement account and funded it with earnings from a summer internship. Since then, she’s continued investing. When she got hired at a management consulting firm after graduating, she contributed to her company’s 401(k) plan and funded her Roth I.R.A. with her annual bonuses. She has an emergency fund that she keeps in money market funds and a separate, passive investment portfolio.

Eventually, she’d like to buy an apartment in a big city. But buying a home isn’t something she is actively saving for, and she doesn’t like the idea of spending money on rent, either. She is currently living with her parents before moving out to start business school later this month.

Rising housing costs and high mortgage rates are making buying a house increasingly less likely to be part of Gen Z’s ticket to building generational wealth. According to a Pew Research Center survey published in June, 89 percent of adults under 40 say it is harder for young adults today to buy a home than it was for their parents’ generation. The survey also showed that young adults are less likely than older ones to say buying a home is a “very good” investment.

Instead, they see saving for retirement, trading on apps and contributing to high-yield savings accounts as their best ways to build wealth.

Though home-buying may feel out of reach, saving for retirement has become one of the biggest financial targets for Gen Z. Research has shown that they are more flexible at pivoting to this form of wealth building than millennials. According to an analysis on retirement savings behavior published earlier this year by Fidelity, Gen Z contributions are increasing 65 percent year-over-year, more than double that of millennials.

“Compared to before when people stayed in their careers longer and companies offered pensions and things like that, I think people have to fend for themselves a little bit more,” Ms. Cummings said. “I’m just trying to be conservative and make sure I have a few different buckets of savings so I’m all set in the future.”

Roberta Katz, a Stanford scholar who has done extensive research on Gen Z and coauthored the book “Gen Z, Explained: The Art of Living in a Digital Age,” said that Gen Z is a generation marked by uncertainty and malleability.

“For Boomers, there was a sense that you have your home, that you build your wealth, that you could build an estate,” Dr. Katz said. “For Gen Z, when we did our study, they did not have any sense of that. One of the things our study found was a very high value for Gen Z on flexibility because there was a belief that the world they were going to know was a world of change.”

Jeff Sharp, 28, works part-time as a bartender while attending flight school to become a pilot. He lives in Bend, Ore., where the median cost of a home has risen to $700,000, nearly 75 percent higher than 20 years ago.

“One of the things that my close friends and I talk about a lot is the difference between what the economy was like for our parents and what the buying power of the U.S. dollar used to be, and what we’re looking at now,” Mr. Sharp said. “There’s still a fair amount of anxiety about how we’re going to be able to reach our financial goals.”

Mr. Sharp started investing in his early 20s, using a trading app, Robinhood, to buy individual stocks. After he learned more about personal finance and decided to follow the best practices of investing in index funds, he switched all of his investments from Robinhood to Vanguard and set up automatic contributions for a Roth I.R.A. and a 529 college savings plan for his daughter. He also uses Acorns, the micro-investing app.

There are now a wide variety of budgeting and investing apps available and Gen Z is eager to learn about their options. A Gallup study earlier this month found that 81 percent of Gen Z adults seek personal finance guidance, with 75 percent finding information online.

Adam Benton, 23, works as head of operations at Titan Dynamics, a defense technology start-up. When he gets his paycheck, he moves a portion of the money into his retirement, brokerage and high-yield savings accounts, using the Charles Schwab app to invest in index funds. He monitors his progress using the net-worth tracker in an app called My Wallet, which shows a graph charting the growth of his wealth.

He saves as much as he can and wants a buy a house one day, but it’s not a goal that feels achievable any time soon.

“It’s so far away, it’s like, what are the odds of ever getting there?” Mr. Benton said. “It is definitely not the same perspective that like my parents have where they say, ‘You have to get into real estate to really build wealth.’”

item.title: Sick of Constant Pings, They’re Sending Texts at the Speed of Carrier Pigeon
item.description:
The carrier pigeon was halfway across the Atlantic Ocean, soaring toward Toronto. Its message, sent from London, would take more than a day to arrive.

But when the letter landed, it was not untied from a spindly leg but rather opened in an app, because this pigeon was digital, not physical.

A lot of time has gone into speeding up human communication, from the telegram to the Pony Express to shouting loudly from a rooftop. Lately, at least two apps have asked: Was a carrier pigeon the pinnacle?

One of the apps exploring this idea is Carrier Pidge, an app that allows users to send messages at the speed of pigeon. Users track their bird on a map as it whips toward its destination.

Like real birds, the digital pigeons have a chance of getting lost or dying — 0.2 percent. Buying a new one within the app will run you 99 cents.

As it turns out, this slower, riskier and costlier version of messaging has wide appeal.

“Some things are better when they’re worse,” said Olivia Macdonald, 27, who uses the app to send messages to her boyfriend. Her texts arrive in minutes — they both live in Manhattan — but the chances of the pigeon disappearing adds intrigue, she said.

“The uncertainty of that, compared to the numbness that we feel receiving so many texts and notifications a day, is something that I just find really attractive about it,” Ms. Macdonald said.

Carrier Pidge, which launched in April, exploded in popularity this month after a post about the app by its developer, Noah Iarrobino, was shared by thousands. After several months with only a couple hundred users, he said, the app now has more than 75,000.

Another app released in April, Roost, which lets users send texts via such animals as including pigeons, snails and penguins, reported that it has reached 650,000 downloads this month.

Both apps have connected with users who are tired of the daily digital grind.

“I was probably inspired by a trend going on in tech — people want to get away from their phones and get outside,” Mr. Iarrobino, 29, said of how the idea came to him. “I thought carrier pigeons were a funny concept, and it would be funny if some of them didn’t make it back.”

Mr. Iarrobino, a software engineer in New York, had developed other apps: One that charges users 99 cents every time they hit snooze on an alarm, another that keeps a leaderboard among users of who touches their phone screen the most in a day.

The first message he sent on Carrier Pidge was to a friend in Chicago — an image of a leotard-clad Danny DeVito from the TV show “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.” Delivery time: 8 hours and 49 minutes.

The speed of each message varies, with a maximum speed of 110 m.p.h. (Mr. Iarrobino said he researched racing pigeons and found one named Bolt that had been recorded at that pace.)

Roost was designed by Logan Mendelsohn, a 31-year-old product manager. Unlike Carrier Pidge, the app offers over 1,000 animals to choose from, with the speeds to match. (A white Italian snail crawls at a little over one mile an hour, while a barn owl flies at about 20 m.p.h.) It has a “pen pal” feature that lets users meet and message new people.

“My focus is leaning in toward the slow-tech movement, leaning into areas that help people around the world connect,” said Mr. Mendelsohn, whose career has been focused on trust and safety in tech. He said Roost has gotten so big that he is planning to hire employees.

There has been some flag-planting in online comments sections from fans of Roost, who accuse Carrier Pidge of copying the concept. But Mr. Mendelsohn and Mr. Iarrobino said in interviews that neither took ideas from the other and that they have discussed their apps with each other.

Their apps appear to have tapped into a palpable discomfort with screen time and constant communication, and a yearning for an antiquated era.

A 2023 survey conducted by the Harris Poll, in partnership with the Human Flourishing Lab at the Archbridge Institute, found that 80 percent of Gen Z adults — those born after 1997 — were worried that their age group relied too heavily on technology. Fifty-eight percent said that new technologies were more likely to drive people apart than unite them.

“A lot of the digital tools that saturate our attention at the moment were built on the idea that friction is bad,” Cal Newport, a professor of computer science at Georgetown University and the author of “Deep Work,” said in an email.

“The human brain cannot function well in a friction-free world,” he said. “Too much information coming at us too fast overwhelms our ability to switch our attention.”

By reintroducing friction through apps like Carrier Pidge and Roost, Mr. Newport said, messages can be thoughtful and given the attention they deserve.

Ema Siddique, 28, deleted most of her social media accounts about five years ago after wondering if constant availability meant that her most important connections were not being tended to enough. When she learned of Carrier Pidge, she saw it as a natural extension of that mind-set.

Her pigeon was the one careening from London, where she lives, to a friend in Toronto (she messages another friend with the app who lives in Kuwait). Ms. Siddique and her friends don’t take the texts too seriously, but quickly began to use old-timey, “Bridgerton”-esque language, referring to one other as “my dearest lady.”

“It’s similar to a letter in the sense that you spend a lot of effort, and it does feel like every word that goes into it is intentional,” Ms. Siddique said.

She added: “You can track it, which adds to the excitement. I have one Carrier Pidge on the way from Kuwait, and you think, ‘What is she going to say in the next one?’”

item.title: The Economy Got Used to Low Borrowing Costs. Their Exit Could Pose Risks.
item.description:
The era of low interest rates is over. The economic hangover is just beginning.

Interest rates on long-term U.S. government debt hit their highest level in nearly 20 years this week, and yields are also rising for government bonds around the world. An intervention by the Treasury Department on Wednesday only fleetingly arrested the rise in rates, which have led to higher borrowing costs for home buyers, businesses and the federal government itself.

Rates are being driven higher by a variety of forces. Stubborn inflation is being exacerbated by the war with Iran and there are questions about how forceful the Federal Reserve will be to tame it. Aggressive borrowing by artificial intelligence companies and hopes that the A.I. boom will lead to faster economic growth in the future. And long-brewing concerns about the federal government’s ability to manage its mounting debt load, which this week topped $40 trillion for the first time.

But beyond the specific explanations, economists say, higher rates are in some ways a return to a more normal period. The real aberration, they say, was the nearly two decades of ultralow rates that followed the global financial crisis in 2008. Average interest rates on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage spent more than a decade below 5 percent, and short-term interest rates were near zero for years. Even now, bond yields remain low by historical standards, especially in inflation-adjusted terms.

“The interest rates of the last couple of decades were unusually low by historical standards, and we’ve now undone that decline,” said Douglas W. Elmendorf, a Harvard economist who led the Congressional Budget Office in the years after the financial crisis. “We’re back up to a level that actually seemed pretty low when we encountered it 20 years ago.”

But the U.S. economy looks very different since the last time rates were at this level. Households and businesses adjusted to a world in which money was cheap. So did the global financial system. Perhaps most significantly, government debt has tripled as a share of economic output over that period.

All of that could make higher rates, however historically normal they may be, much more painful this time around.

“We got somewhat spoiled,” said Tara Sinclair, an economist at George Washington University who worked in the Treasury Department during the Biden administration. “A lot of our financial systems were pretty substantially reworked around this assumption of pretty low interest rates.”

Higher rates also pose a political problem for President Trump, who campaigned on a promise to improve affordability for inflation-weary Americans. Instead, mortgage rates, which fell during Mr. Trump’s first year back in office, are rising again, and interest rates on auto loans, credit cards and other forms of consumer debt remain elevated.

Mr. Trump spent months haranguing the Fed to slash borrowing costs, and this year appointed a new chairman, Kevin M. Warsh, who he believed would do so. But stubborn inflation, partly a result of Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran, has taken cuts off the table. Investors now think the Fed is more likely to raise rates this year than anything else.

But even if Mr. Trump were to have gotten his wish, the Fed only directly controls short-term interest rates. What matter most to the economy are long-term rates, which help determine what it costs to borrow money to buy a house or build a factory. Those rates are set by market forces as investors buy and sell government bonds. When fewer people want to lend the government money, or demand a higher return for doing so, interest rates rise.

For much of the past two decades, investors’ appetite for U.S. government debt seemed insatiable. They poured money into government bonds during the 2008 financial crisis, when hardly any other asset seemed safe. They kept buying during the anemic economic recovery that followed, when pension funds, wealthy individuals and other savers had more cash on hand than there were attractive places to invest it.

The Fed was also a voracious buyer of government debt, as it turned to untested measures to shore up the economy by keeping a lid on borrowing costs. By ensuring strong demand for Treasury bonds, policymakers pushed up prices and put downward pressure on long-term interest rates. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

The United States, and to a lesser degree its peers around the world, took advantage of the opportunity to borrow cheaply, running large deficits even as the economy improved. Despite giving occasional lip service to the need for fiscal responsibility, Republicans and Democrats alike continued to cut taxes and increase spending.

Then came the Covid-19 pandemic, which shut down whole sectors of the economy and left tens of millions of people out of work. The federal government responded in dramatic fashion, providing trillions of dollars in aid to households and businesses — virtually all of it borrowed money. So did the Fed, which bought unlimited quantities of government debt and a range of other securities.

Economists largely cheered the aid efforts, although some warned that the final spending package, under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., was larger than it needed to be and would ultimately fuel inflation. Investors showed no hesitation, either, snapping up the debt at rock-bottom interest rates.

But many economists argued that the federal government should rein in deficits once the crisis passed. That didn’t happen. The tax-and-spending bill that Mr. Trump signed last year will add more than $4 trillion to the deficit over the next decade, according to the latest estimate from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office.

Investors’ concerns about the federal government’s fiscal trajectory are contributing to the recent rise in bond yields, said Hanno Lustig, an economist at Stanford University who has studied the Treasury market. For decades, investors paid a premium — in the form of a lower yield — for the safety and liquidity provided by government bonds. Today, that premium has largely disappeared.

The problem, Mr. Lustig added, is that deficits that looked sustainable when interest rates were lower now look much less so.

“Now, you’re left with a fiscal position that was constructed for a low-rate regime that is gone, at least for now,” he said.

Already, the Congressional Budget Office estimates that the federal government will spend more than $1 trillion on interest payments this year, more than it spends on any program other than Social Security or Medicare. That figure is expected to rise sharply over the next decade even if interest rates remain relatively stable.

If, instead, interest rates continue to rise, that will push up the cost of servicing the debt, which will make the fiscal picture look even worse. That, in turn, could spook investors, leading them to demand still higher returns for the risk of lending the government money — a self-perpetuating cycle known as a fiscal crisis.

Few economists think such a crisis is imminent. But they say the risks are rising.

“Economists cannot predict when a crisis will occur because it’s not just a matter of a single number on the debt clock,” Mr. Elmendorf said. “It is people’s perceptions of a government’s ability to manage its finances.”

Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, argued on Thursday that the United States could grow its way out of its debt problem.

Economists acknowledge that there are new sources of growth, such as those stemming from the A.I. boom. But the pace at which the debt has compounded makes catching up hard to do. Those A.I. companies have also flooded the market with a torrent of new debt as they seek to fund their expansion plans, in effect competing with the government for a limited pool of investor capital.

What is more, faster growth tends to lead to higher interest rates, though for benign rather than troubling reasons.

The bottom line: The era of low rates is unlikely to return anytime soon.

For the Fed, that could mean that the “neutral rate” — the interest rate that neither speeds up growth nor slows it down — is higher than in the recent past. Most policymakers now estimate that the neutral rate is just above 3 percent, up from 2.5 percent before the pandemic.

With the economy on steady footing and inflation too high for the central bank’s liking, the primary debate that has divided policymakers is whether the overnight rate that the Fed sets — currently at a range of 3.5 percent to 3.75 percent — is applying any restraint on the economy.

If the answer is yes, the Fed can feel confident that inflation will over time ease back to its 2 percent target, a goal it has been missed now for half a decade. But if the answer is no, the central bank faces pressure to act, or risk contributing to an even more persistent inflation problem.

Policymakers who have called for higher borrowing costs — of which there are now several — point to the economy’s resilience as a clear sign that rates are too low.

“If you just observe the real economy backdrop and you observe the markets, it tells you that rates aren’t restrictive,” said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM. He thinks the Fed should raise rates by 0.75 percentage points over its next three policy meetings before pausing to assess how the economy is faring. Absent that, Mr. Sockin said, the Fed should feel “no confidence” that inflation would return to the 2 percent target anytime soon.

These doubts have injected yet more uncertainty into the bond market, contributing in part to the move higher in long-run interest rates. If inflation remains high and the Fed does not act, bond investors will demand higher returns to compensate them.

As such, some investors argue that a Fed that is more aggressive in stamping out inflation could over time help to keep a lid on longer-term rates.

The urgency around rate rises, however, will depend in large part on the incoming economic data.

“If inflation doesn’t slow, the empirical evidence builds that there is not enough monetary policy restraint to bring inflation to the target,” said Roger Hallam, global head of rates at Vanguard. “The data has to provide the rationale for them not to raise rates.”
